## About the course

MTH 317H is an advanced introduction to linear algebra and abstract vector spaces,
with a strong emphasis on mathematical communication. Students learn to construct
logical arguments and write clear, rigorous proofs.

The course has two lecture sections that meet on Tuesdays and Thursdays and cover the
linear algebra. I lead the **Monday recitations**. For roughly the first half of the
semester, recitation is an accelerated introduction to proof writing (essentially the
content of MTH 299), taught through notes and collaborative worksheets. Later
recitations practice the linear algebra from lecture. Many recitations start with a
short quiz.

**Learning objectives**

- Understand and use key concepts of linear algebra: vector spaces, linear
  transformations, systems of linear equations, determinants, and
  eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
- Gain proficiency in constructing and writing proofs.

**Texts (all free online, except the last two)**

- Sheldon Axler, *Linear Algebra Done Right*, 4th ed. (LADR)
- Sergei Treil, *Linear Algebra Done Wrong* (LADW)
- Richard Hammack, *Book of Proof*, 3rd ed.
- Kevin Houston, *How to Think Like a Mathematician*
- Chartrand, Polimeni and Zhang, *Mathematical Proofs: A Transition to Advanced Mathematics*

## How recitations work

Each session aims to have students *predict, explore, and sometimes fail productively*
before they prove, and then consolidate what they found in short notes. A typical
packet includes:

- a **warm-up** that surfaces the key idea, such as sorting maps by whether they are
  injective or surjective;
- **proof frameworks**: the first and last lines of a proof of "injective",
  "surjective", "not injective", and so on;
- **investigations** that turn computed examples into conjectures;
- **"grade the proof"** tasks, where students find and repair common logical errors;
- an **exit ticket** to check understanding at the end of class.
